cards.title: Advertorial Definition and Credibility Transfer
cards.summary: An advertorial is a paid advertisement formatted as editorial content so readers transfer the host publication's trust to your brand.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to buy sponsored-placement content on a publisher, newsletter, or platform versus running a standard display or social ad for a product.
steps: Recognize that most shoppers distrust obvious ads but still extend trust to editorial articles that mention a company favorably; an advertorial combines advertisement plus editorial into one piece.
Secure placement in a publication your audience already trusts (examples the source cites: Forbes, The Wall Street Journal, Time, BuzzFeed, Thrillist, The New York Times).
Format your placement to read like the host's normal content rather than a display unit, so readers process it as editorial.
Accept that the mechanism is a credibility transfer: readers subconsciously treat 'it's in [publication], so it must be legit' as endorsement.
Expect this to be controversial with journalists and some readers; disclose sponsorship where required and weigh reputational risk against reach.
For ecommerce, use advertorials mainly for top-of-funnel discovery of a product category or brand, then route readers to a PDP or landing page to convert.
caveats: The source flags genuine controversy: borrowing publication trust can backfire if readers feel deceived.
Sponsorship may be only a small label (e.g., 'sponsored by'), so many readers won't consciously notice it—this is the intended effect but also the ethical risk.

cards.title: The 70/30 Content-to-Pitch Ratio
cards.summary: Write advertorials as roughly 70% genuinely useful or entertaining content and 30% or less promotional pitch so people read, engage and share them.
cards.use_when: Writing any sponsored article, advertorial, paid newsletter placement, or top-of-funnel content piece intended to drive product discovery and sharing.
steps: Adopt a giving mindset: the goal is content people like, engage with, and share—not a blatant ad nobody will pass along (the source's 'spammy Sarah' vs 'giving Gary' contrast).
Allocate roughly 70% of the piece to high-quality value: benefits and how-to use the product, cool features, stories, or entertainment.
Keep the actual sales pitch to about 30% or less of the piece; the source says AppSumo's sample deal spent under 30% of the email selling.
Aim for content that is at least as good as the host publication's own editorial—the source argues 'giving Gary' strives to beat the publication's normal quality.
If you pay for placement, remember the ad dollars only pay off if people finish the article and share it, so the value portion protects your spend.
Apply the same ratio to the promotional email or landing page you send advertorial traffic to; keep the offer clear but don't flip to 100% pitch.
caveats: 70/30 is the source's working heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
The source doesn't give a formula for measuring the split—treat it as a writing/editing guide.

cards.title: AppSumo's Daily Deal Email Structure
cards.summary: AppSumo's daily deal emails to ~750,000 subscribers led with a story or how-to rather than a hard sell, keeping the promo under ~30%.
cards.use_when: Designing promotional emails or sponsored placements for a deal, bundle, or product launch to a large list where unsubscribes and low open rates are a risk.
steps: Don't send emails that just repeat 'buy this'—the source says blatant daily promotions get unsubscribed from immediately.
Craft a great story or a how-to guide built around the product as the bulk of the email.
Spend the majority of the email on how to use the product, its benefits, and its cool features for buyers.
Cap the actual deal pitch at under ~30% of the email—the source shows a sample AppSumo deal where less than 30% of the content sold the deal.
Expect this structure to produce more full reads, more shares, and more purchases than a pure promotion, and fewer unsubscribes.
Use the same principle for ecommerce launch or deal emails: lead with useful/entertaining content connected to the product, then place the offer.
caveats: The 750,000-subscriber figure and the 'more engagement' claim are the source's account of AppSumo's own results, not a guaranteed benchmark.

cards.title: The Tear-Out Benchmark (Ogilvy)
cards.summary: David Ogilvy's advertorials succeeded because they were useful enough that readers physically tore them out to keep as reference.
cards.use_when: Judging whether a piece of sponsored or content-marketing material is valuable enough to earn saves, shares and repeat exposure for a product.
steps: Judge advertorial usefulness by the tear-out standard: would a reader rip this out of a magazine and keep it because it benefits them?
Make the content itself a functional reference—the source cites Ogilvy's Rinso detergent ad that homemakers kept in their laundry rooms as a stain-removal guide.
For a second Ogilvy example, the source cites a Guinness oyster-pairing guide that restaurants displayed so patrons could use it.
Note the source's claim that the Rinso ad outperformed other detergent ads of its era specifically because it was tear-out-able and useful.
For ecommerce, translate the tear-out test into saveable/shareable assets: buying guides, size or compatibility charts, care or usage references tied to your product category.
Design the piece so the brand mention is present but the reference value stands on its own—usefulness is what drives the extra reach.
caveats: The historical results (e.g., 'did better than any other detergent ad ever') are the source's retelling, not verified data.
This is a historical magazine-era example; the modern ecommerce application is the adapting recommendation, not the source's demonstrated result.

cards.title: Build Shareability With Listicle and Fun-Content Sponsored Posts
cards.summary: Sponsors gain reach by paying for entertaining, shareable listicles that are only loosely related to the product, not direct product ads.
cards.use_when: Planning a top-of-funnel sponsored placement on a listicle site or social platform when direct product ads get scrolled past.
steps: Look at how major brands sponsor fun or loosely related content: the source cites Captain Morgan sponsoring a BuzzFeed listicle about captains, and TGI Fridays sponsoring a Thrillist piece on 'worst office lunches.'
Note the source's point that people won't share an article about how great a restaurant is, but they will share '13 worst office lunches ever' with coworkers—the fun angle drives sharing.
Pick content angles your audience would genuinely share even without the brand, then work the brand mention in naturally (e.g., the restaurant featured as a good place to eat).
Expect social engagement to be the payoff: the source claims silly listicle-style advertorials can generate millions of views and tens of thousands of shares.
Convert this reach by routing readers to your PDP, offer or landing page rather than leaving the mention as exposure only.
For a dog-food example, the source suggests turning a standard 'Donnie loves Purina puppy chow' ad into a shareable piece like '21 dogs that have been working out way too hard.'
caveats: The millions-of-views and tens-of-thousands-of-shares figures are the source's illustration, not a promise for your placement.
Loose relevance means weak intent—measure downstream conversion, not just views and shares.

cards.title: Warm Up Cold Audiences Before the Direct Ad
cards.summary: A standard ad converts poorly unless the surrounding content is already about your product's category, so advertorials prime readers first.
cards.use_when: Deciding between a direct response ad and a sponsored-content placement, or sequencing top-of-funnel content before a product page for cold traffic.
steps: Recognize that a plain 'Donnie loves Purina puppy chow' ad with a Buy button can work, but the source says it generally converts at a very low rate.
Identify the exception: a direct ad performs far better when the article or page someone is already reading is directly about the topic (e.g., 'what's the best dog food').
When you can't control the surrounding content, use an advertorial to put your product in a relevant, trusted editorial context instead.

Even indirect mention works for exposure: the source notes an article about Purina being named the number-one brand or its stock growing still gets the name out there and can drive purchases, even though it's not about the product.
Sequence this as top-of-funnel priming: advertorial or sponsored content warms the audience, then a retargeting ad or landing page captures the purchase.
Match ad format to placement relevance—use direct-response units where context already matches intent, sponsored content where it doesn't.
caveats: The source gives the low-conversion claim as a general observation without benchmarks or data.
Indirect brand exposure (stock/company news) is weaker for conversion than product-relevant content.

cards.title: Actively Demonstrate the 70/30 Split (the Source's Exercise)
cards.summary: The source demonstrates building an advertorial by converting a bare 'product + Buy button' ad into a 70% value / 30% pitch piece.
cards.use_when: Workshopping or briefing a sponsored article draft for a product when your current creative is a flat product-plus-buy-button ad.
steps: Start from your standard ad: product claim, image, Buy button—recognize this as the baseline the source contrasts against.
Decide where the placement lives (e.g., a publication like The Wall Street Journal, or a BuzzFeed-style listicle) and write to that publication's editorial voice.
Draft the bulk (~70%) as content readers would want on its own merits—a story, how-to, or funny list—using the source's dog-food example of a viral 'dogs working out too hard' piece.
Insert the product mention into the content honestly and naturally (e.g., the product as a feature within a broader fun or useful piece), keeping the pitch portion to ~30% or less.
Add the promotional element—a deal, a link, a store mention—after the value has been delivered.
Test the resulting piece against the tear-out and shareability tests: would someone save it or send it to a friend?
Route advertorial readers to a conversion page (PDP or landing page) and measure reads-to-clicks-to-purchases separately from the article's engagement.
caveats: The walkthrough is a teaching exercise, not a documented ecommerce campaign result.
The source's 'Donnie the dog / Purina' scenario is hypothetical and does not imply a real brand relationship.

input.source_name: Advertorials_ How To Write Them & Why They’re Awesome.docx
input.text:
11-ADC / ad copy Goes here. A breakdown of advertorials (sponsored content), detailing how to disguise advertisements as editorial content using a 70% value / 30% promotion ratio, with historical and modern examples. Not here. • Email marketing or automated email sequences -> 14-EML • Website landing page optimization -> 07-LPG • Tracking, analytics, or attribution -> 06-MEA

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Explains the strategy and psychology behind sponsored content and advertorials, providing a clear ratio for blending organic value with paid promotion to bypass consumer ad blindness and increase shareability. modules: [ADC] topics: [advertorials, sponsored content, native advertising, David Ogilvy, copywriting, AppSumo, top-of-funnel marketing] tier: 3 scope_hint: overview

Topics. the definition of an advertorial / explaining that it is an advertisement disguised as a regular piece of editorial content designed to bypass consumer distrust of blatant ads by borrowing the credibility of the host publication (e.g., The New York Times, Forbes); the 70/30 rule / the foundational mindset of making an advertorial 70% high-quality, valuable, or entertaining content and only 30% sales pitch to ensure it gets shared and engaged with rather than ignored; AppSumo's email strategy / using the 70/30 ratio in daily deal emails to 750,000 subscribers by focusing the bulk of the email on stories or how-to guides related to the product rather than just saying "buy this"; modern examples of native advertising / analyzing how major brands sponsor seemingly unrelated or fun content to gain exposure, such as Fidelity sponsoring an article on pension buyouts on Forbes, Captain Morgan sponsoring a listicle about captains on BuzzFeed, or TGI Fridays sponsoring a "worst office lunches" article on Thrillist; the David Ogilvy approach / referencing historical successes where Ogilvy created highly useful advertorials (like the Rinso detergent reference guide or the Guinness oyster pairing guide) that housewives and restaurants would physically tear out of magazines to keep; creating a viral advertorial / demonstrating how to turn a standard display ad for dog food into a shareable piece of content (e.g., "21 Dogs Working Out Too Hard") to generate millions of views and massive social engagement; the credibility transfer / noting the controversy in journalism surrounding advertorials because readers subconsciously transfer the trust they have in the publication directly to the sponsored brand.

Look for.

The 70/30 Rule: The core formula for writing an advertorial: 70% of the content must be highly valuable, useful, or entertaining editorial content, while only 30% (or less) is the actual promotional pitch.

The "Tear-Out" Benchmark: The historical standard set by David Ogilvy for advertorials, where the content is so useful (like a stain removal guide from a detergent company) that consumers physically tear it out of the publication to keep for reference.

Borrowing Credibility: The psychological mechanism of native advertising where a brand bypasses consumer skepticism by associating its message with the trusted reputation of the host publication (e.g., Wall Street Journal or Forbes).

Skip. The intro/outro promotional hooks for "Copywriting Course" and the hypothetical thought exercise about "Donnie the Dog."

Scope mix. 60% baseline (definitions of advertorials and sponsored content), 40% growth (applying the 70/30 rule to drive viral engagement). Volume. ~400 words.
